questions.q: A polished 300 mm prime wafer costs ~$100-150 when it enters a leading-edge fab and is worth ~$17,000-20,000 when it leaves ~3 months later. Which single factor best explains where that value was added?
options: The silicon was purified further inside the fab, from 9N to 11N
Roughly 1,000-1,500 process steps across ~70-100+ mask layers were performed on tools from a fab costing ~$20-30B, with most capex in equipment
The wafer was thinned from 775 um to ~30 um, which is the most expensive step
The fab embedded HBM memory into the wafer during the BEOL
questions.explanation: The fab adds value through the ~1,000+ patterning, deposition, etch, implant, and CMP steps that build transistors and ~15-18 wiring levels, amortizing a $20-30B facility whose cost is ~70-80% equipment. Purity is fixed before the fab; thinning and HBM integration happen afterward, in packaging.

questions.q: In the module's illustrative H100 SXM bill-of-materials model, which listed component contributes the largest estimated hardware cost?
options: The 814 mm2 GPU die (~$350 at ~45-50 sellable die per ~$16.5k wafer)
The five HBM3 stacks (80 GB at ~$15-20/GB, roughly $1,200-1,600)
Wafer sort and final test
The SXM printed circuit board and voltage regulators
questions.explanation: In this illustrative model, HBM has the largest listed component cost. These are estimates for a historical configuration, not disclosed purchasing prices or a measured NVIDIA product gross margin.

questions.q: TSMC reports total wafer capacity across many nodes. Why does that number alone fail to identify the bottleneck for a particular AI accelerator?
options: All process nodes and package types are interchangeable
A package needs appropriately allocated logic wafers, memory and packaging capacity; the smallest compatible output can constrain shipments
Only the raw silicon mass matters
Foundry capacity measures finished GPU racks
questions.explanation: Total 12-inch-equivalent capacity does not disclose the relevant node, allocation, yield or package and memory availability. Bottlenecks must be assessed for the actual product and period.

questions.q: A planning example assumes 100,000 wafer starts per month, 24 EUV passes per wafer, and 100,000 productive passes per scanner per month. How many scanners cover that nominal workload?
questions.explanation: The demand is 2,400,000 passes per month. Divide by 100,000 productive passes per scanner to obtain 24 scanners. Real plans additionally account for the assumptions behind availability, dose, maintenance and reserve capacity.

questions.q: Which set correctly names the three chokepoints of the leading-edge supply chain as described in this module?
options: Quartz mining, metallurgical-grade silicon smelting, and polysilicon purification
EUV lithography (ASML), leading-edge foundry (TSMC in Taiwan), and advanced packaging plus HBM (CoWoS; SK hynix/Samsung/Micron)
EDA software, CPU IP licensing, and server ODM assembly
Copper supply, ultrapure water, and data-center electricity
questions.explanation: Each of these three is a step where one or a handful of firms hold nearly all capability: ASML is the sole EUV supplier, TSMC makes >90% of the most advanced logic wafers, and CoWoS capacity and HBM output gated AI accelerator supply. Raw silicon is cheap and abundant.

questions.q: In the master process flow, 'replacement metal gate' (gate-last) comes AFTER which of these steps, and why?
options: After M1 dual damascene, because the gate is formed in the BEOL
After source/drain epitaxy and ILD0 CMP, because the dummy polysilicon gate must survive the high-temperature S/D epi and anneal steps before being swapped for high-k and work-function metals
Before STI formation, because the gate defines the active area
After wafer sort, because the gate metal is deposited during bumping
questions.explanation: In a gate-last flow, a sacrificial amorphous-Si dummy gate is patterned first, spacers and embedded S/D epi are formed around it, ILD0 is deposited and polished to expose it, and only then is it removed and replaced with the HfO2 high-k stack, work-function metals, and W/Co fill, so the metals never see the S/D thermal budget.

questions.q: A component BOM is estimated at $3,000 and a reseller quotes $30,000 for a GPU module. Which conclusion is justified?
options: NVIDIA has a verified 90% product gross margin
NVIDIA spends $27,000 on R&D per unit
The component estimate is 10% of the reseller quote, but realized revenue and full cost of revenue are needed to calculate gross margin
The silicon wafer costs $30,000 per die
questions.explanation: A BOM can omit manufacturing overhead, testing, warranty and other costs; the reseller quote need not equal manufacturer revenue. The arithmetic gap is not a disclosed margin.

questions.q: A GPU and its HBM stacks need thousands of wires between them in a strip a few millimetres wide. Which carrier can route wiring at the ~1 um pitch this requires, and what is it called in a CoWoS package?
options: The printed circuit board (~50-100 um line pitch), called the baseboard
The ABF build-up substrate (~10 um pitch), called the core
A slab of silicon wiring with no transistors (~1 um pitch), called the interposer
The copper NVLink spine (~1 mm pitch), called the bridge
questions.explanation: Every carrier has a minimum wire spacing: a PCB ~50-100 um, an ABF substrate ~10 um, a silicon interposer made with fab lithography ~1 um, the chip itself <0.1 um. Only silicon-class patterning can route thousands of GPU-to-HBM wires in a few millimetres, so a silicon (or fine-RDL) interposer sits between the dies and the organic substrate; that is the "wafer" in Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate.
